text: dsh-tm-guard 是面向 DSH 的 macOS 工作区权限门控与文件回滚插件，通过 tools/pre-execute 拦截工具调用，并提供系统提示和 tm_* 工具。它记录允许或拒绝的操作，创建 Time Machine 快照，并支持查看状态、审计记录及回滚文件。适合希望在 DSH 会话中管理本地写入和检查点的用户；需要 macOS、APFS、Time Machine 与 git，插件不要求 API 密钥或外部账号。

dsh-tm-guard gates DSH tool calls and records allow or deny decisions. Its tm_* tools create and list Time Machine snapshots, inspect audit history, and restore files. Intended for macOS DSH workspaces; it requires APFS, Time Machine, and git, with no API key or external account.

dsh-tm-guard 的功能「工具调用审计」：在 DSH 工具执行前接入门控，并提供 tm_audit 查看近期允许或拒绝记录、目标路径和快照标识。可按最近条数筛选，也可只查看写操作。
dsh-tm-guard 的功能「快照与文件恢复」：通过 tm_snapshot 创建带备注的 Time Machine 本地快照，并可用 tm_rollback 按路径和快照日期恢复文件，或指定最近一次操作相关文件进行回退。

dsh-tm-guard README · dsh-tm-guard：**A zero-intervention permission gate for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH) agents on macOS — active on install.** Writes that can be undone via a local git baseline or macOS Time Machine are auto-approved and automatically snapshotted; network access, package installs, process/system management, and reads of sensitive credential paths are blocked; every decision is audited — the audit log keeps everything by default, with optional automatic cleanup of the oldest records.

dsh-tm-guard README · dsh-tm-guard：> Core rule: **operations that can be rolled back are allowed; operations that cannot be rolled back are denied.**

---

dsh-tm-guard README · Quick Start (2 minutes)：1. **Install**: `dsh plugin --profile <name> add dsh-tm-guard` (see [Installation](#installation)).
2. **Verify it loaded**: boot the profile — the console prints `[tm-guard] Loaded. Protected paths: ...` (see [Verify the install](#verify-the-install)).
3. **Protect your workspace**: defaults already protect `process.cwd()`, deny network/system operations, and block reads of 12 sensitive credential paths. To protect more directories, add `protectedPaths` to your profile's `cordis.patch.yml` ([Configuration](#configuration)).
4. **Unlock the tools you explicitly trust**: `subagent`, `workflow`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `skill`, ... are **DENIED by default** (classified `mixed`/`unknown`). Add the ones you trust to `extraAllowTools` in your profile's `cordis.patch.yml`. ⚠️ Never add `subagent` / `subagent_fork` / `workflow` / `job_output` — the allow-list short-circuits the classifier (see [Limitations](#limitations--honest-scope)).

dsh-tm-guard README · Quick Start (2 minutes)：> The two fields that change the experience most: `protectedPaths` (what the agent may write) and `extraAllowTools` (which tools bypass the gate). Everything else has a safe default.

dsh-tm-guard README · What this is — and isn't：**It is** a DSH [Cordis](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/cordis) **plugin / bundle**: an npm package (`dsh-tm-guard`) that declares `dsh.bundle.patch`, hooks DSH's `tools/pre-execute` waterfall, registers `tm_*` model tools, and injects an operating-mode system-prompt section. It installs with the official `dsh plugin add` flow and runs inside the DSH host process with the host's permissions.

**It is not:**

dsh-tm-guard README · What this is — and isn't：- a Claude Code plugin (no Claude Code plugin manifest or Claude Code hooks),
- a VS Code extension,
- a standalone CLI or product,
- **a security sandbox** (see [Limitations & honest scope](#limitations--honest-scope)).

---

dsh-tm-guard README · Prerequisites：- **macOS** with APFS. The plugin shells out to `/usr/bin/tmutil` and uses local APFS snapshots; there is no non-macOS support.
- **Time Machine configured** with a backup destination, and the workspace on a TM-backed volume that is **not** in Time Machine's exclusion list. Verify:

```sh
  tmutil destinationinfo
  tmutil listlocalsnapshots /
  ```

dsh-tm-guard README · Prerequisites：- **Full Disk Access** granted to the terminal/app that runs `dsh` (needed for browsable-backup restore and some `tmutil` operations), if you want automated rollback from completed backups. Local snapshot creation itself needs no sudo on normal user volumes.
- **`git` on PATH** for the primary instant rollback net (a local baseline is auto-created per writable directory; all git operations are local/offline).
- **DSH CLI installed**, matching the peer range in `package.json` — currently `@deepseek-ai/cordis >=4.0.0` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools >=0.1.0-rc.1 <0.1.0 || >=0.1.0 <0.1.2-0 || >=0.1.2-0 <0.2.0-0 || >=0.2.0-0 <0.3.0-0` (covers dsh 0.1.x including `0.1.2-rc.1` and dsh 0.2.x including `0.2.0-rc.2`).

dsh-tm-guard README · Installation：A DSH profile installs out-of-tree bundles via `dsh plugin --profile <name> ...` (forwarded to pnpm inside the profile directory). Choose any profile name, e.g. `web` or a throwaway `tm-lab`.

dsh-tm-guard README · From npm (recommended)：Prebuilt `lib/` ships in the package, so no build step or build-script approval is needed:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-tm-guard
```

If the install fails on the build-script approval, add the key pnpm prints to the profile's `pnpm-workspace.yaml`:

and re-run the command. Treat that allowance as permission to run the package's code at install time on your machine; pin a commit when auditing supply chain: `github:ChaoJie0/dsh-tm-guard#<sha>`.

dsh-tm-guard README · How it works：```
agent tool call
      │
      ▼
ctx.on('tools/pre-execute')   ← registered with prepend: runs FIRST

Three decision classes:

dsh-tm-guard README · How it works：1. **Local, reversible** — reads; writes under `protectedPaths`; local/offline git (`init/add/commit/reset/checkout/restore/clean/stash/...`); recognized local executors. Allowed. A git baseline is ensured before the first write and an APFS snapshot is taken (throttled by `snapshotCooldownSeconds`).
2. **Irreversible / non-local** — network commands (`wget`, `ssh`, `git push/pull/clone/fetch`), package managers (`npm/pip/brew/cargo/... install`), process/system management (`kill`, `sudo`, `launchctl`, `shutdown`), subagent delegation, catastrophic patterns (`rm -rf /`). Denied. **`curl` exception:** a *strict read-only GET* that writes the response body to a local file (`curl [-sSL] https://… -o file`, or `-O/--remote-name`) is treated as a reversible **file write**, not as network egress: it is allowed when the output file is under `protectedPaths` (a git/APFS restore point is taken), inside the session workspace (a git baseline is auto-created on the first write — no manual setup), or under a temp dir (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/var/folders`); writes elsewhere are denied, and `curl` to stdout (no `-o/-O`) is denied as network. Any POST/upload, custom

dsh-tm-guard README · How it works：Anything unrecognized is denied by default (conservative). For locally executed interpreter scripts, the plugin additionally performs a **static, read-only** egress scan of the entry file, inline `-c`/`-e` code, and heredoc bodies — and follows local imports a few levels deep — flagging real outbound requests or unverifiable `eval/exec/__import__`.

dsh-tm-guard README · How it works：**Rollback.** Local git is the primary mechanism (instant, offline, root-free, covers tracked files and files created after the baseline). Time Machine is the disaster-recovery backstop. `tm_rollback` tries, in order: (1) copy from a browsable completed TM backup (`tm-backup`, needs Full Disk Access), (2) mount the local APFS snapshot (`manual-mount`, needs root), and (3) print exact manual instructions (`manual`).

dsh-tm-guard README · How it works：**Audit & reports.** Every allow/deny is appended to `<workspace>/.tm-guard/audit.jsonl` (tool, category, reason, target paths, snapshot id). After each agent turn with tool activity, a structured Markdown report with an independent acceptance check is written to `.tm-guard/reports/turn-<timestamp>.md`. When `autoApprove` is on (default), the plugin answers DSH approval requests with `allowed-once` for calls the prepended gate already permitted — that is what makes runs prompt-free; only pre-approved calls can reach that stage.

dsh-tm-guard README · Registered tools：| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `tm_snapshot` | Create a Time Machine local APFS snapshot checkpoint; takes a `note` label, returns the snapshot date id. |
| `tm_list_snapshots` | List available local snapshots with dates, for choosing a rollback point. |
| `tm_rollback` | Restore an explicit `path` (optionally at `snapshot_date`), or `last_operation=true` to undo the most recent write recorded in the audit log. |
| `tm_audit` | Show recent gate decisions (allow/block, category, target paths, snapshot ids); `limit`, `only_writes`. |
| `tm_status` | Print TM health/destination/snapshot count, workspace protection, gate policy, and audit-log stats. |
| `tm_backup` | Start a backup to the configured TM disk; background by default, `wait=true` blocks for a browsable restore point. |
| `tm_backup_status` | Show whether a backup is running, percent complete, and current phase. |

dsh-tm-guard README · First-run baseline report：On the **first** `apply()` in a workspace — detected by `.tm-guard/baseline-report.md` not existing — the plugin writes `.tm-guard/baseline-report.md` and prints one line pointing at it. The report answers the question a fresh install otherwise cannot: **what protection level am I actually in right now?**

It contains six sections, each a read-only probe of *this* machine:

dsh-tm-guard README · First-run baseline report：| # | Section | What it reports |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Time Machine 配置 | `tmutil destinationinfo` result, workspace TM-protection, overall TM health |
| 2 | Workspace 保护状态 | the effective writable scope, and which paths TM's exclusion list misses |
| 3 | Git baseline 可建性 | whether `git` is on PATH and the directory is already a work tree |
| 4 | denyReadPaths 实际生效项 | the effective count and the full list, with the merge semantics in force |
| 5 | 平台支持状态 | `full mode` on macOS, `limited mode` elsewhere |
| 6 | 已知残余风险 | the residual risks from [Limitations](#limitations--honest-scope), restated on your machine |

dsh-tm-guard README · First-run baseline report：- **Read-only.** The git probe runs `git rev-parse` and stops. It does **not** call `git init`, does **not** commit, does **not** create a snapshot, and does **not** touch your config. The report says so itself, and section 3 states that the baseline is created lazily at your first write. (This is why the report can be generated at load time without mutating the workspace.)
- **Generated once, kept.** Later `apply()`s do a single `existsSync` and leave the file alone — the report is a first-run *snapshot*, not a live view. If your Time Machine setup changes afterwards, the file keeps showing what was true at first run; use `tm_status` for the live answer. To regenerate, delete the file and restart the session.
- **Never fatal.** If the report cannot be written, `apply()` logs a warning and the gate loads normally. A display artifact must never stop the safety mechanism it describes.
dsh-tm-guard README · First-run baseline report：`tm_status` echoes the path in its 【Data sources】 section, so the report is discoverable from the tool a user reaches for when something looks wrong.

dsh-tm-guard README · Auto-approval and its blast radius：When `autoApprove` is `true` (the default), the plugin answers DSH approval requests with `allowed-once` on your behalf — that is what makes unattended runs prompt-free. The safety argument for this is narrow and worth stating plainly:

dsh-tm-guard README · Auto-approval and its blast radius：- The `tools/pre-execute` gate is registered with **`prepend`**, so it classifies and denies *before* any other listener can raise an approval `ask`. Only operations that already passed the gate reach the approval stage.
- If another permission plugin registers earlier in the waterfall, or bypasses the gate entirely, an operation could reach that stage **without** having been checked — and it would still be auto-approved. This plugin cannot verify the ordering of plugins it does not control.

dsh-tm-guard README · Auto-approval and its blast radius：For that reason the plugin prints a startup warning whenever `autoApprove` is `true`, telling you to check the ordering if you run it alongside other permission plugins. Set `autoApprove: false` to let approval asks reach the user (or fail closed) instead.

dsh-tm-guard README · Auto-approval and its blast radius：There is one combination with **no backstop at all**: `failClosed: false` (writes are no longer blocked when no rollback net exists) together with `autoApprove: true` (the human prompt that would have caught it is auto-answered). The plugin warns specifically about this pair at startup. Keep `failClosed: true` unless you have a deliberate reason not to.

---

dsh-tm-guard README · Configuration：The plugin accepts a `Partial<TmGuardConfig>` on its inserted row. Users normally override fields from their own profile's `cordis.patch.yml` (later patch layers win per row; a patch replaces the whole row `config`).

dsh-tm-guard README · Configuration：| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `protectedPaths` | `string[]` | `[process.cwd()]` | Absolute path prefixes writable by the agent. |
| `snapshotCooldownSeconds` | `number` | `30` | Min seconds between automatic pre-write APFS snapshots. `0` snapshots before every write; negative disables auto-snapshot. |
| `denyNetwork` | `boolean` | `true` | Deny classified network operations. |
| `denySystem` | `boolean` | `true` | Deny process/system-management commands. |
| `denyReadPaths` | `string[]` | credential/keychain paths listed above | Absolute or `~`-prefixed paths the agent may not read. **Additive by default**: entries are appended to the built-in list ([Sensitive paths](#sensitive-paths)), so you cannot accidentally drop the defaults by listing one path. `[]` adds nothing. |
| `denyReadPathsReplace` | `boolean` | `false` | When `true`, `denyReadPaths` **replaces** the built-in sensitive-path list instead of being appended to it. Replacement is the fail-open direction — the dropped defaults are named in a startup warning — so set this only when you are curating the whole list deliberately. |
| `extraAllowTools` | `string[]`

dsh-tm-guard README · Configuration：| `auditMaxBytes` | `number` | `0` | Per-file audit rotation threshold in **bytes** (default `0` = rotation off, the audit log keeps everything). Set a positive value (e.g. `10485760` = 10 MiB) to enable rotation: when the live `audit.jsonl` would exceed it, the current content is rotated to `.1` and a fresh file starts. See [Audit log rotation](#audit-log-rotation). |
| `auditRetainFiles` | `number` | `5` | How many rotated generations (`.1`, `.2`, …) are kept before the **oldest is physically deleted**. Total retained ≈ `auditMaxBytes × (1 + auditRetainFiles)`. |
| `auditTotalMaxBytes` | `number` | `104857600` | Optional global cap in **bytes** (default 100 MiB) across all generations; a safety net if `maxBytes`/`retainFiles` are raised. |

dsh-tm-guard README · Configuration：> **⚠️ Do NOT put `subagent` / `subagent_fork` / `workflow` / `job_output` in `extraAllowTools`.** The allow-list short-circuits classification entirely, so a whitelisted subagent tool bypasses the gate's `mixed`-category denial and can write outside `protectedPaths` without rollback coverage. Subagents are `mixed` by default and denied for exactly that reason; keep them out of the allow-list (see Limitations).

dsh-tm-guard README · Configuration：Example — your profile's `cordis.patch.yml` (the shipped bundle itself inserts a bare row; this is how a user configures it):

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: tm-guard
      name: dsh-tm-guard
      config:

dsh-tm-guard README · Audit log rotation：Since 0.2.6 the audit log **keeps everything by default** — rotation is off, so
an unattended machine's full history is retained. Rotation is **opt-in** for
users who prefer bounded disk usage: set `auditMaxBytes` (per-file threshold in
**bytes**, e.g. `10485760` = 10 MiB); `auditRetainFiles` is optional and
defaults to 5 generations. With 10 MiB × 5 generations the total is ≈ 50 MiB
(100 MiB hard cap).

dsh-tm-guard README · Audit log rotation：- Rotation is **pre-append**: the triggering record lands in the fresh file,
  and `.1` is byte-for-byte the pre-rotation history.
- **The oldest generation is physically deleted** once the retained window is
  full — this is a real, intentional trade-off (0.2.4 had an unbounded log;
  0.2.5 rotated by default; 0.2.6 made rotation opt-in).
  Rollback/forensics reach back only as far as the retained window.
- Cross-process lock keeps several hosts from corrupting the same file.
- **To enable rotation** (bounded disk usage — only for users who prefer a cap
  over full history): set `auditMaxBytes: 10485760` (10 MiB); `auditRetainFiles`
  defaults to 5 if omitted.
- **To keep more history** without going unbounded, raise both, e.g.
  `auditMaxBytes: 104857600` (100 MiB) + `auditRetainFiles: 20`
  (≈ 21 × 100 MiB retained).
- Each rotation is recorded through the plugin's structured logger under the
  name `tm-guard` (visible in the host log surface; e.g. web profile:
  `/tmp/dsh-web.log`), and the current generation count is always readable via
  `tm_status` → 【Data sources】. Rotation is a normal self-healing event — it
  does not interrupt or

dsh-tm-guard README · Audit log rotation：```yaml
config:
  auditMaxBytes: 0              # default: rotation off, keep everything
  # or
  auditMaxBytes: 10485760       # bytes per file (10 MiB, rotation on)

dsh-tm-guard README · Sensitive paths：`denyReadPaths` is a list of **prefixes**. Every entry matches the path itself and everything beneath it, so `~/.ssh` covers `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/config` and so on. A match denies the operation whether the path is being read *or* written — the list protects credentials from being overwritten, not just read.

The built-in list ships with the plugin (source of truth: `src/sensitive-paths.ts`, exported as `DEFAULT_SENSITIVE_PATHS`):

dsh-tm-guard README · Sensitive paths：| Group | Paths | What it protects |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud & shell credentials | `~/.ssh`, `~/.ssh/config`, `~/.aws`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.kube`, `~/.docker`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.config` | Private keys, cloud CLI credentials and SSO token caches, GPG keyrings, kubeconfig bearer tokens, registry auth, plaintext HTTPS tokens. `~/.config` is the XDG base directory (`gh`, `gcloud`, `heroku`, …). |
| Agent & CLI credentials | `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `~/.cursor`, `~/.codex`, `~/.claude.json`, `~/.claude`, `~/.gemini`, `~/.aider.conf.yml`, `~/.continue` | Credential stores belonging to the agent/CLI tools this plugin runs alongside — the GitHub CLI OAuth token, and the auth/session state of the Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Gemini, Aider and Continue tooling. These are long-lived tokens for *other* execution surfaces, so an autonomous agent reading them widens its own blast radius. |
| Platform keystores | `~/Library/Keychains`, `~/Library/Cookies` | The macOS login/System keychain databases and browser session cookies. |

dsh-tm-guard README · Adding your own paths (additive by default)：`config.denyReadPaths` is **appended** to the built-in list, so a profile can add a project-specific secret location without weakening anything:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: tm-guard
      name: dsh-tm-guard
      config:

This is deliberate. The earlier semantics replaced the whole list, so a profile that appended one path silently dropped *every* cloud and agent credential entry — a fail-open change disguised as a small config tweak.

text:
dsh-tm-guard README · Platform support：The plugin probes `process.platform` at load time.

On **macOS (`darwin`)** it runs in **full mode**: local APFS snapshots, `tmutil` health checks, rollback strategies and the fail-closed Time Machine backstop are all active.

On **any other platform** there is no `tmutil`, so the plugin runs in **limited mode** rather than pretending otherwise:

dsh-tm-guard README · Platform support：- A one-line `console.error` states the platform is unsupported and that the gate is running in "no Time Machine rollback net" mode — write protection rests on the **git baseline only**.
- The gate **does not block writes** for absence of a TM net (there is none to check); the TM-health fail-closed check and every `tm_*` snapshot/rollback path are inert. The git baseline is still created and committed before writes exactly as on macOS.
- A `console.warn` restates the degradation **once per apply()** the first time a write is approved, so a long unattended run cannot forget it. It is deliberately not repeated per call — a warning that fires constantly is one users learn to ignore.
- `tm_status` reports `platform: <platform> — limited mode (no TM)` and marks TM health `N/A — no TM on this platform (git baseline is the rollback net)` instead of the misleading `UNHEALTHY — writes BLOCKED`.
- The **first-run baseline report** labels section 5 `limited mode（无 TM）`, names the git baseline as the only rollback net, and renders section 1 as "TM 不适用 … 能力限制，不是故障" — it never claims a Time Machine destination or health it cannot have. This is pinned by tes

dsh-tm-guard README · Platform support：The point of stating this loudly is that **silent degradation is the dangerous outcome in a safety tool**. Before this probe, a non-macOS user saw a handful of failing `tm_*` tools while the gate still spoke fail-closed language about Time Machine protection — easy to read as "a rollback net exists" when none did. If you need real rollback guarantees, run on macOS with Time Machine configured, or use a disposable VM/profile.

---
dsh-tm-guard README · Limitations & honest scope：Please read this before trusting the plugin. It raises the bar for unattended runs; it is not a proof of isolation.

dsh-tm-guard README · Limitations & honest scope：- **macOS + Time Machine only.** Everything on the snapshot side depends on `/usr/bin/tmutil`, APFS local snapshots, and a configured TM destination. There is no Linux/Windows path. Local snapshot creation is sub-second, but mounting a fresh local snapshot back for command-line restore needs root or the Time Machine UI — prefer the git baseline for instant undo. On a non-macOS host the plugin still loads and still gates, but degrades to **limited mode** — see [Platform support](#platform-support).
- **Full Disk Access matters.** Without it, automated restore from completed TM backups (`tm-backup` strategy) cannot read the backup; the plugin falls back to root-required mounting or printed manual steps.
- **The static egress scan has blind spots.** It is a regex/text analysis, not execution tracing. URLs assembled at runtime, `eval(decodedBytes)`, targets hidden behind Makefiles or `cargo run`, or code in unscanned transitive files are not caught. `denyNetwork=true` also does not prevent a determined actor from using an allowed channel.
- **It is not a kernel-level sandbox.** The plugin runs as trusted host code with the DSH process's

dsh-tm-guard README · Development：The build is **zero-dependency**, using Node's built-in TypeScript type-stripping (`module.stripTypeScriptTypes`). Build machine requirement: **Node.js ≥ 22.6 (or ≥ 20.19 LTS)**. The emitted `lib/` is plain ESM JavaScript plus a hand-maintained `lib/index.d.ts`; consumers need no TypeScript toolchain.

```sh
npm run build      # node scripts/build/build.mjs → lib/
npm run prepare    # alias of build; run automatically on npm/git installs
```

Project layout:

dsh-tm-guard README · Development：```text
src/
  index.ts         # plugin entry: pre-execute gate, hooks, system prompt, tm_* tools
  classifier.ts    # tool mapping + bash segment parser + decision matrix
  scan-scripts.ts  # static egress scan for interpreter scripts / inline code / heredocs

Smoke tests are dependency-free Node scripts importing the TypeScript source (Node strips types at import time; same Node version requirements as the build):

dsh-tm-guard README · Development：```sh
node --experimental-strip-types test-classifier.mts
